title: The pause button
intro: Your first real crash as a SIP investor. The reader who wrote the story hovered exactly here — steer, and watch the compounding meter.

nodes.text: Markets are down sharply. Your SIP debits tomorrow. The portfolio number is red, friends are quoting scarier numbers, and the pause button is right there.

choices.label: Pause the SIP until things look clearer
choices.note: You just converted a plan into a series of timing calls.

choices.label: Let it run — this is what the plan was built for
choices.note: Tomorrow's debit buys more units than any debit this year.

nodes.text: Three months later the market has recovered half the fall — without you. 'Clearer' never announced itself. Re-entry now means buying higher than you paused.

choices.label: Restart the SIP and write down what the pause cost
Wait for the retest of the bottom before restarting
choices.note: Now you're a market timer with no plan at all.

nodes.text: The fall deepens another 8% before turning. Your cost basis kept dropping the whole way. At recovery, the units bought in the trough are the portfolio's best performers. Then life adds its own test:

choices.label: Continue — and step the SIP up with this year's raise
choices.note: The step-up habit compounds the discipline.

nodes.text: A real emergency arrives — six figures, this month. Where does the money come from?

choices.label: The emergency fund you kept outside the long-term corpus
choices.note: The SIP never even noticed the emergency.

choices.label: Redeem long-term equity — it's all one pot anyway
choices.note: The emergency just taxed your compounding at the worst time.

ending.principle: The SIP's job is to keep buying when you least want to; liquidity's job is to make sure nothing forces its hand.
ending.debrief: Both reader stories in one run: the almost-paused SIP that kept buying cheap units, and the liquidity pillar that absorbed the shock without touching the plan. Neither required prediction — only structure set up before the test arrived.

ending.principle: A plan raided in emergencies and paused in falls is not a plan — it's a mood with a folio number.
ending.debrief: The meter's arithmetic was consistent: every choice that made the plan contingent on feelings or events cost integrity. The fixes are structural, not motivational — pre-commitment for the SIP, a separate liquidity floor for the shocks.
